exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices

question.text:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

\[ \bf{U}=\begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & 0.7 \\ 0.9 &0.3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{V}=\begin{bmatrix} 0.45 & 0.35 \\ 0.25 & 0.65 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{W}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

  • Matrix $\bf{U}$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}0.1 & \color{purple}0.7 \\ \color{blue}0.9 & \color{purple}0.3 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \begin{array}{l} \color{blue}0.1 + 0.9= 1 \\ \color{purple}0.7 + 0.3 = 1 \end{array} \end{align*}

  • Matrix $\bf{V}$ is not a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): \[ \begin{bmatrix} \color{red}0.45 & 0.35 \\ \color{red}0.25 & 0.65 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Matrix $\bf{W}$ not a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \color{red}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & \color{red}0 & 0 \\ 0 & \color{red}0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\bf{U}$ only."

question.text:
Which of the following are stochastic vectors?

\[ \bf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0 \\ 0.5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} -0.45 \\ 1.55 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{w}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our vectors in turn.

  • Vector $\bf{u}$ is a stochastic vector. Indeed,

    • its entries are all nonnegative, and

    • the entries add up to one: \[ 0.5+0+0.5 = 1 \]

  • Vector $\bf{v}$ is not a stochastic vector since it contains negative entries.

  • Vector $\bf{w}$ is not a stochastic vector since the entries do not add up to one: \[ 0+0 = 0 \neq 1 \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\bf{u}$ only."

Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

\[ \bf{U}=\begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{V}=\begin{bmatrix} 0.45 & 0.25 \\ 0.55 & 0.75 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \bf{W}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.7\end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1.$ A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

  • Matrix $\bf{U}$ is not a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): \[ \begin{bmatrix} \color{red}0.2 & 0 \\ \color{red}0.5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Matrix $\bf{V}$ is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}0.45 & \color{purple}0.25 \\ \color{blue}0.55 & \color{purple}0.75 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \begin{array}{l} \color{blue}0.45 + 0.55 = 1 \\ \color{purple}0.25 + 0.75 = 1 \end{array} \end{align*}

  • Matrix $\bf{W}$ is not a stochastic matrix since its second column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): \[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \color{red}1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & \color{red}0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.5 & \color{red}0 & 0.7\end{bmatrix} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\bf{V}$ only."

exampleAnswers.title: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data

question.text:
There are three cable TV providers in a particular apartment block: provider $A,$ provider $B,$ and provider $C.$ A study has shown that, each year

  • from the tenants using provider $A,$ $80\%$ swap to provider $B$ and $10\%$ swap to provider $C,$

  • from the tenants using provider $B,$ $25\%$ swap to provider $A$ and $25\%$ swap to provider $C,$

  • from the tenants using provider $C,$ $70\%$ swap to provider $A$ and $10\%$ swap to provider $B.$

The stochastic matrix that describes this situation is given below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} & 0.25 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We are given the following situation for each year:

  • From the tenants using provider $A,$ $80\%$ swap to provider $B$ and $10\%$ swap to provider $C.$ This implies that $10\%$ of them continue using provider $A.$

  • From the tenants using provider $B,$ $25\%$ swap to provider $A$ and $25\%$ swap to provider $C.$ This implies that $50\%$ of them continue using provider $B.$

  • From the tenants using provider $C,$ $70\%$ swap to provider $A$ and $10\%$ swap to provider $B.$ This implies that $20\%$ of them continue using provider $C.$

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

From:
Provider A Provider B Provider C
To: Provider A $0.1$ $0.25$ $0.7$
Provider B $0.8$ $0.5$ $0.1$
Provider C $0.1$ $0.25$ $0.2$

We can write the corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:

\[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{0.25} & 0.7 \\ 0.8 & 0.5 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{0.1} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{0.1} & 0.25 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we have

\[ a+b+c = 0.25 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.45. \]

question.explanation:
We are given the following situation for each month:

  • From the customers that prefer chain $A,$ $ 5\%$ change to chain $B$ and $15\%$ change to chain $C.$ This implies that $80\%$ of them continue to prefer chain $A.$

  • From the customers that prefer chain $B,$ $25\%$ change to chain $A$ and $25\%$ change to chain $C.$ This implies that $50\%$ of them continue to prefer chain $B.$

  • From the customers that prefer chain $C,$ $15\%$ change to chain $A$ and $35\%$ change to chain $B.$ This implies that $50\%$ of them continue to prefer chain $C.$

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

From:
Chain A Chain B Chain C
To: Chain A $0.8$ $0.25$ $0.15$
Chain B $0.05$ $0.5$ $0.35$
Chain C $0.15$ $0.25$ $0.5$

We can write the corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:

Finally, we have

\[ a+b+c = 0.25 + 0.05 + 0.5 = 0.8. \]

example.title: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data

question.text:
\[ P= \begin{bmatrix} 0.35 & 0.15\\ 0.65 & 0.85 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_0= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider a Markov chain with the stochastic matrix $P$ and the initial state vector $\mathbf{x}_0$ given above. Calculate the state vector $\mathbf{x}_2.$
question.explanation:
To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_2,$ we apply two steps of the Markov chain: \[ \mathbf{x_1}=P\mathbf{x}_0, \qquad \mathbf{x}_2=P\mathbf{x}_1 \]

After the first step, we have

\begin{align} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0.35 & 0.15\\ 0.65 & 0.85 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.7 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.21 \\ 0.79 \end{bmatrix} . \end{align}

Finally, after the second step, we obtain

\begin{align} \mathbf{x}_2 &= P \mathbf{x}_1 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.35 & 0.15\\ 0.65 & 0.85 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.21 \\ 0.79 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.192 \\ 0.808 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix and Making a Prediction

question.text:
A certain company produces three types of ground coffee: fine, medium, and coarse. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between the three types of ground coffee each year:

From:
Fine Medium Coarse
To: Fine $0.5$ $0.2$ $0.2$
Medium $0.3$ $0.6$ $0.4$
Coarse $0.2$ $0.2$ $0.4$

For example, $30\%$ of fine ground coffee customers switch to medium ground coffee each year, and $20\%$ of coarse ground coffee customers switch to fine ground coffee.

Currently, $300\,000$ customers buy fine ground coffee, $500\,000$ customers buy medium ground coffee, and $200\,000$ customers buy coarse ground coffee. How many customers will purchase fine ground coffee in one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
question.explanation:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

\[ P=\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.2\\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 &0.2 &0.4 \end{bmatrix} \]

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of ground coffee is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 300\,000 \\ 500\,000 \\ 200\,000 \end{bmatrix}. \] Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

\[ \mathbf{x}_0 = \dfrac{1}{1\,000\,000}\begin{bmatrix} 300\,000 \\ 500\,000\\ 200\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.5\\ 0.2 \end{bmatrix} \]

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0 \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.2 & 0.2\\ 0.3 & 0.6 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 &0.2 &0.4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.5\\ 0.2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}0.29 \\ 0.47 \\ 0.24 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, after one year, $\color{blue}29\%$ of customers will buy fine ground coffee. Computing $29\%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

\[ 1\,000\,000 \cdot 0.29 = 290 \, 000. \]

Therefore, $290\,000$ customers will buy fine ground coffee in one year.

example.title: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix and Making a Prediction

question.text:
A certain company produces $2$ types of flour, flour $A$ and flour $B.$ The following table describes how the number of consumers changes between both types of flour each month:

From:
Flour $A$ Flour $B$
To: Flour $A$ $0.3$ $0.6$
Flour $B$ $0.7$ $0.4$

That is, $70\%$ of flour $A$ customers switch to flour $B$ each month, and $60\%$ of flour $B$ customers change to flour $A.$

Currently, $6\,000$ customers use flour $A,$ while $4\,000$ customers use flour $B.$ How many customers will use flour $A$ in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
question.explanation:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

\[ P=\begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \]

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of flour is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 6\,000 \\ 4\,000 \end{bmatrix}. \] Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(10\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

\[ \mathbf{x}_0 = \dfrac{1}{10\,000}\begin{bmatrix} 6\,000 \\ 4\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \]

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0 \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.3 & 0.6 \\ 0.7 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}0.42 \\ 0.58 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, after one month, $\color{blue}42\%$ of customers will use flour $A.$ Computing $42\%$ of $10\,000,$ we obtain

\[ 10\,000 \cdot 0.42 = 4\,200. \]

Therefore, $4\,200$ customers will use flour $A$ in one month.

From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

\[ P=\begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.3\\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 &0.4 &0.5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of instant soup is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 400\\ 400 \\ 200 \end{bmatrix}. \] Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

\[ \mathbf{x}_0 = \dfrac{1}{1\,000}\begin{bmatrix} 400 \\ 400\\ 200 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 \\ 0.4\\ 0.2 \end{bmatrix} \]

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one month, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0 \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.3\\ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 &0.4 &0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 \\ 0.4\\ 0.2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0.3 \\ 0.32 \\ \color{blue} 0.38 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, after one month, $\color{blue}38\%$ of customers will buy vegetable soup. Computing $38\%$ of $1\,000,$ we obtain

\[ 1\,000 \cdot 0.38 = 380 . \]

Therefore, $380$ customers will buy vegetable instant soup in one month.

question.text:
A certain company produces two types of smartphones: Phone $A$ and Phone $B.$ The following table describes how the number of customers changes between both types of smartphones each year:

From:
Phone $A$ Phone $B$
To: Phone $A$ $0.6$ $0.3$
Phone $B$ $0.4$ $0.7$

That is, $40\%$ of Phone $A$ customers switch to Phone $B$ each year, and $30\%$ of Phone $B$ customers switch to Phone $A.$

Currently, $600\,000$ customers use Phone $A,$ while $400\,000$ customers use Phone $B.$ How many customers will use Phone $A$ in one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
question.explanation:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

\[ P=\begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \]

The vector describing the number of customers for each smartphone is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 600\,000 \\ 400\,000 \end{bmatrix}. \] Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

\[ \mathbf{x}_0 = \dfrac{1}{1\,000\,000}\begin{bmatrix} 600\,000 \\ 400\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \]

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0 \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \color{blue}0.48 \\ 0.52 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, after one year, $\color{blue}48\%$ of customers will use Phone $A.$ Computing $48\%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

\[ 1\,000\,000 \cdot 0.48 = 480 \, 000. \]

Therefore, $480\,000$ customers will use Phone $A$ in one year.

question.text:
A certain company produces two types of footwear: casual and sports. The following table describes how the number of customers changes between both types of footwear each year:

From:
Casual Sports
To: Casual $0.55$ $0.7$
Sports $0.45$ $0.3$

That is, $45\%$ of casual customers switch to sports each year, and $70\%$ of sports customers change to casual.

Currently, $700\,000$ customers purchase casual footwear, while $300\,000$ customers purchase sports footwear. How many customers will purchase sports footwear in one year? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.
question.explanation:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

\[ P=\begin{bmatrix} 0.55 & 0.7 \\ 0.45 & 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \]

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of footwear is \[ \begin{bmatrix} 700\,000 \\ 300\,000 \end{bmatrix}. \] Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers $(1\,000\,000),$ we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

\[ \mathbf{x}_0 = \dfrac{1}{1\,000\,000}\begin{bmatrix} 700\,000 \\ 300\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 \\ 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \]

To find the state vector $\mathbf{x}_1$ after one year, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

\[ \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0 \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}_1 &= P \mathbf{x}_0 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0.55 & 0.7 \\ 0.45 & 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 \\ 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 0.595 \\ \color{blue}0.405 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, after one year, $\color{blue}40.5\%$ of customers will purchase sports footwear. Computing $40.5\%$ of $1\,000\,000,$ we obtain

\[ 1\,000\,000 \cdot 0.405 = 405 \, 000. \]

Therefore, $405\,000$ customers will purchase sports footwear in one year.
